methods.label: Compare the region with the hexagon
methods.explanation:
Connecting the six indicated centers gives the regular hexagon. Comparing the enclosed region with this hexagon will let us add the outward circular portions and subtract the inward ones.

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12A_Q14_question_fig1.svg)

The boundary has three outward lobes, each containing two congruent arcs, and three inward portions, each containing one. Let \(r\) be their common radius and \(\theta\) the central angle of one arc, measured in degrees. The arc-length formula gives
\[
\frac{\theta}{360^\circ}\,2\pi r=\frac{2\pi}{3},
\qquad r\theta=120^\circ.
\]
We first determine \(r\), without assuming that neighboring circles are tangent.

At a junction \(P\) between arcs with adjacent centers \(U,V\), we have \(UP=VP=r\) and \(UV=2\). Therefore \(2\leq2r\), so \(r\geq1\) and \(\theta\leq120^\circ\).

Suppose \(r>1\). The triangles formed by two adjacent centers and their arc junction all have side lengths \(r,r,2\), so they are congruent. Let their common positive base angle be \(\delta\). Each endpoint radius therefore makes an angle \(\delta\) to one side or the other of its corresponding hexagon side.

A regular hexagon has interior angle \(120^\circ\). For the inward portion, adjusting its two endpoint rays changes this angle by \(-2\delta\), \(0\), or \(2\delta\). For the outward lobe, the reference sweep is the complementary \(240^\circ\), with the same three possible adjustments. But \(r>1\) gives \(\theta<120^\circ\) and \(2\theta<240^\circ\). Thus both sweeps would have to use the negative adjustment:
\[
\theta=120^\circ-2\delta,
\qquad
2\theta=240^\circ-2\delta.
\]
Doubling the first equation and comparing with the second forces \(\delta=0\), a contradiction. Hence \(r=1\), and \(\theta=120^\circ\).

Adjacent centers are now distance \(2\) apart with their common junction distance \(1\) from each, so each junction is the midpoint of a hexagon side. The enclosed region is consequently the hexagon, together with three outward \(240^\circ\) sectors, with three inward \(120^\circ\) sectors removed. These added sectors lie outside the hexagon, and the removed sectors lie inside it, with disjoint interiors.

Joining the hexagon's center to its vertices divides it into six equilateral triangles of side \(2\). Each has altitude \(\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3\), so the hexagon has area \(6\sqrt3\). Therefore the required area is
\[
6\sqrt3
+3\left(\frac{240}{360}\pi\right)
-3\left(\frac{120}{360}\pi\right)
=\boxed{\pi+6\sqrt3},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
